raw_response:
I've been working this land for 35 years. I know Quzhou's soil — it's calcareous, tends to dry out fast. My 6 mu isn't much, and it's just me running it, so I can't afford mistakes or fancy experiments. I do what I know works.

My whole farm runs on wheat-maize rotation. Wheat in winter, maize in summer, same ground, year after year. That's how it's done here on the North China Plain. My well gives me irrigation control which is the most important thing — Hebei summers can be brutal and winters are dry.

**Wheat:** I sow in mid-October, harvest in June. I've been using the same improved variety for years — a local one that my neighbors and I trust. I'm not chasing whatever new variety the seed shops push. I rotary till after I pull the maize — the stalks need to go under. I irrigate three times: once before winter sets in to help root establishment, once at jointing in April, once at heading. That's been my pattern. I spread base fertilizer before sowing — phosphorus and potassium down, part of the nitrogen — then topdress nitrogen at jointing. Two rounds of pesticide: herbicide in early spring, then something for powdery mildew and aphids around flag leaf stage. I can reliably get 450 kg/mu on this land.

**Maize:** I sow right after wheat harvest in June, no-till directly into the stubble — saves me time and the soil holds moisture better. Maize is hybrid, always has been, everyone around here uses hybrid. Fertilizer base goes in at sowing, then I topdress heavily at the big-bell stage when the plant really needs it. I irrigate at seedling if it's dry and again at tasseling if there's no rain. Two pesticide passes: herbicide early, then borer control mid-season. I expect around 550 kg/mu.

One person, 6 mu, well irrigation — this plan is what I can manage and what I've proven to myself over decades.
